resources.string: Right form, wrong meaning
name + name: the parser accepts
semantics
Until now, the parser checked the form. A plus ok has the right form: name, plus, name. But ok is a bool, true or false.
Adding a number to true or false makes no sense. Who reports this error? Tap it.
The scanner and the parser only look at the form. The form here is right.
Semantic analysis. It checks the meaning, and it is the subject of this region. The first step is knowing the type of each piece.
Look at the tree: the operator sits in the node, and there is no E, T or F. It is the lean tree, with only operations and values. You learn to build it two lessons from now.
On the machine, adding integers and adding reals are different instructions.
If a and x are float, which instruction does this addition? Tap it.
Read what is under each instruction. Look for adding floats.
The add dot s. The instruction changes with the type, so the compiler must know the type first.
To pick the right instruction, the compiler must know the type of each piece of the expression.
ATTRIBUTE
An attribute is a piece of information attached to a tree node, such as its type or value. The rules that compute it come with the grammar.
Type checking goes up from the leaves to the root, one node at a time.
1. A number with a dot is float. No dot, int.
2. Variable: type comes from the symbol table.
3. One float child gives float. Else, int.
4. Comparison gives bool. Bool in math: error.
In the first example, x was float. Which rule said so? Tap it.
x is a variable. Where does its type live?
Correct. The declaration of x was in the table.
In step three, the int that meets a float is coerced: it becomes float before the operation.
Another expression. The leaves already have types, from rules one and two.
What is the type of c times two? Tap it.
Both children are int. Neither is float.
Integer with integer stays integer.
And at the root, integer plus real? Tap the type.
Rule three: one float child is enough.
The integer becomes real before the sum.
Now ok, which is bool, took the place of y. What type goes up?
Rule four: bool does not go into arithmetic.
Exactly. The root gets a type error.
The error goes up to the root, and the compiler reports it. In the practice step, you see the other kind of attribute: the inherited one, which goes down.
Two functions each declare a variable i. Each one wants its own.
A use of i inside g refers to which declaration? Tap it.
Look for the declaration between the braces of g.
The float i, declared inside g. The int i of f does not count there.
At every use of i, the compiler must find the right declaration.
The scope of a declaration is the part of the program where it holds. In C, it is the block where it was made.
Each block has its own table. The recipe takes care of their stack.
1. Block opens: push an empty table.
2. Declared: write the name in the top table.
3. Use: search from the top. Not found, error.
4. Block closes: pop its table.
The inner x hid the outer one. Which rule did that? Tap it.
Think about where the search starts.
Nice. The search stops at the first x it finds.
Rule four: the block closed, and the names declared in it vanish together.
Now you do the search. The outer block already has its table.
outer: %1$s
inner: %1$s
The inner block opened. On the lit line, which table answers?
The search starts at the top. Is the name there?
The inner table has that name.
And on this lit line? Tap the table where the search stops.
The top does not have that name. The search goes down.
Only the outer table knows that name.
Here comes the brace that closes the block. Which table leaves the stack?
Rule four: the table of the closed block leaves.
You got it. The inner table leaves.
The print uses the only table left, the outer one.
The processor does one operation at a time, always with two values.
processor
one operation at a time
How many operations are on this line? Tap the number.
Count the operators. Each one is an operation.
Two operations, so two lines.
First the syntax tree. It already says which operation comes first.
To generate the lines, walk the tree from the bottom up.
1. Generate the children before the parent.
2. Each operator gets a new temporary.
3. The parent uses the child's temporary.
4. Assignment: copy the last temporary.
Why did the times come out before the plus? Tap the rule.
In the tree, the times is a child of the plus.
Child before parent.
Rule three: on the second line, t1 takes the place of the times.
Now you generate. At the end, the result goes into x.
Which operator becomes t1? Tap it.
The multiplication waits for both children. Start with the left child.
The sum becomes t1.
The sum became t1. Which operator becomes t2? Tap it.
The multiplication is still waiting for its right child.
Correct. The subtraction becomes t2.
Now the root. Tap the line the times generates.
Rule three: use the children's temporaries.
Three addresses: t3, t1 and t2.
We still need to store into x. Which temporary goes there? Tap it.
Rule four: the last temporary, the root's.
The last line just copies the value.
Four lines, and none does more than one operation. In the practice step, if and while also become lines, with labels and jumps.
This line runs a thousand times inside a loop.
As it is, how many times does the program compute two times three? Tap it.
The operation is inside the loop. How many times does the loop run?
A thousand times, once per pass. And the result is always six.
Each operation done ahead saves a thousand when the program runs.
OPTIMIZE
To optimize is to replace the code with faster or smaller code that gives exactly the same result.
Folding walks the tree, from the leaves up to the root.
1. Numbers only: swap in the result.
2. Go up: the result may complete a parent.
3. With a variable, it waits for run time.
In the first example, the sum with y stayed. Which rule says so? Tap it.
y only has a value when the program runs.
Nice. The variable holds the operation for later.
Step two makes one fold trigger another: the result becomes a new constant.
Without optimizing, this expression becomes three lines. Let's fold.
Which operation does the compiler fold first? Tap the operator.
Look for an operator with two numbers below it.
Two times three becomes six.
The six went up. Which operation now has only numbers? Tap it.
Rule two: look at the parent of the six.
Ten minus six becomes four.
Four times x is left. Tap the only line the program runs.
x only exists when the program runs. That operation stays.
You got it. One line instead of three.
The result is the same for any x. Only the path got shorter. Other classic optimizations: copy propagation and dead code elimination.
The function fat calls itself, with a smaller n.
If n lived in a single place, which value would be lost? Tap it.
The new call writes over the old one.
The fat of two would lose its n.
RECORD
Each function call gets its own block on the run-time stack: the activation record.
The fat of one calls no one. It returns one right away.
Calling and returning always follow the same recipe.
1. Call: push the record (parameters, return).
2. Only the record on top is running.
3. Return: pop and go to the return address.
The fat of one went back to the fat of two. Which rule? Tap it.
The record left, and control went back.
Rule three: pop and go back.
Rule one: the return address goes into the record, together with n. That is how the function knows where to go back.
Another program. Main called f with c equal to one.
Which function does f call first? Tap it.
Read the line of f from left to right.
Correct. g gets a record on top of f.
g calls h with b times two. What is the value of a? Tap it.
b is one. One times two is how much?
Exactly. The record of h keeps a equal to two.
How many records are on the stack now, counting main? Tap it.
Count the boxes, from main to the top.
One record per call that has not returned yet.
h and g have returned. Which record runs now? Tap it.
Rule two: only the top runs.
Nice. f runs again from where it stopped.
f calls h again. A new record, now with a equal to one.
In the end, f returns five to main.
Reading memory is slow. Registers are fast, but there are few.
Where does the operation run faster? Tap it.
The register is inside the processor.
That is why every value wants a register.
Deciding which value stays in which register is register allocation.
The recipe starts at the code and ends at the colors.
1. Liveness: who will still be read below?
2. Interference: link who lives together.
3. Colors: neighbors differ. No color, spill.
The wire between the first two variables came from which step? Tap it.
The wire links whoever lives at the same time.
Interference becomes a wire in the graph.
Liveness analysis runs backwards, from the last line to the first.
Now with real temporaries. Four lines, four temporaries.
Start from the bottom. Right after the lit line, who is still live? Tap the temporaries.
Live means it will still be read further down. t2 is read on this line, and nobody reads it after.
Correct. t1 and t3 coexist, so they get a wire.
Now go up one line. And right after this lit line? Tap whoever is live.
t1 will still be read further down. And who did this line just create?
Exactly. One more wire, from t1 to t2.
How many registers are enough for this graph? Tap the number.
t2 and t3 have no wire between them.
Two are enough, with no spill.
Four temporaries in two registers. Nobody went to memory.
